name: Technologies: data stores
description: PostgreSQL, Redis, SQLite and Drizzle, vector databases.

groups.gg: data store fact in our projects

cards.subject: A relational store
says: organises data in tables of rows and columns linked by keys
queries data with SQL
enforces a schema declared up front
cards.use: need joins and constraints across well-structured records
not: stores each record as a self-describing blob with no shared structure

cards.subject: A document store
says: keeps each record as a self-contained JSON-like document
lets documents in one collection differ in shape
reads a whole aggregate such as an order with its lines in one fetch
cards.use: keep an aggregate together and read it as one unit
not: requires every document to match one fixed table definition

cards.subject: A key-value store
says: maps a key to an opaque value and looks values up by that key
offers little beyond lookups by key and does not query by value contents
scales simply because every operation touches one key
cards.use: need the fastest possible lookup by a known key
not: supports joins between values by default

cards.subject: A wide-column store
says: groups values into column families addressed by a row key
is built to spread huge write volumes across many nodes
lets rows in the same table have different columns
cards.use: ingest massive write volumes with queries known in advance
not: is the same thing as a columnar analytics store

cards.subject: A columnar analytics store
says: stores each column's values together on disk
reads only the columns a query names
compresses well because neighbouring values are similar
cards.use: scan and aggregate a few columns over billions of rows
not: is optimised for updating single rows many times per second

cards.subject: A graph database
says: stores entities as nodes and relationships as edges
follows relationships without expensive join chains
answers questions such as friends of friends efficiently
cards.use: traverse many-hop relationships between connected records
not: is the best choice for summing a column over every row

cards.subject: An in-memory store
says: keeps its working data in RAM
answers in far less time than a disk-bound database
needs a persistence plan or accepts losing data on restart
cards.use: serve data that must be read in a fraction of a millisecond
not: keeps data safe across a power cut without any configuration

cards.subject: An object store
says: stores whole files as objects addressed by a key
suits large blobs such as images and backups
does not support editing part of an object in place
cards.use: keep uploads, exports and backup files
not: supports SQL joins between objects

cards.subject: Polyglot persistence
says: uses a different store for each job inside one system
adds operational work for every extra store
needs a clear owner of truth for each fact
cards.use: see one system with documents, cache and search needs
not: means copying the same data into every store as equal masters

cards.subject: MVCC
says: keeps several versions of a row so readers do not block writers
gives each transaction a consistent snapshot
leaves dead row versions that must later be cleaned up
cards.use: explain why a long read does not block updates in PostgreSQL
not: locks the whole table for every read

cards.subject: A jsonb column
says: stores JSON in a decomposed binary form
can be indexed and queried by key or path
does not preserve key order or duplicate keys
cards.use: need flexible fields inside a relational row
not: stores the original text exactly with its whitespace

cards.subject: A GIN index
says: maps each element or key to the rows that contain it
speeds containment queries on jsonb and arrays
is the usual index behind full-text search
cards.use: need to query inside jsonb, arrays or text
not: is the default index created for every primary key

cards.subject: Autovacuum
says: runs in the background to reclaim dead row versions
refreshes the statistics the planner uses
leaves dead rows piling up as table bloat when it falls behind
cards.use: see a heavily updated table growing without new data
not: rewrites the table to defragment the disk every night

cards.subject: The PostgreSQL write-ahead log
says: records each change before the data files are updated
is replayed to recover after a crash
feeds streaming replication and point-in-time recovery
cards.use: explain how PostgreSQL survives a crash mid-write
not: is a text log meant only for humans to read

cards.subject: A PostgreSQL extension
says: adds types, functions or index methods installed with CREATE EXTENSION
is how vector similarity search is added to PostgreSQL
must be installed per database
cards.use: want PostgreSQL to store and compare embeddings
not: is a separate server process that PostgreSQL proxies to

cards.subject: A connection pooler
says: shares a small set of server connections among many clients
protects PostgreSQL, which spends a process on every connection
can break session features in transaction pooling mode
cards.use: see many app instances exhausting database connections
not: makes each query run faster by caching its plan on the client

cards.subject: LISTEN and NOTIFY
says: lets sessions send messages through the database on named channels
delivers only to sessions connected at that moment
needs no extra broker for light signalling
cards.use: want a lightweight signal between processes already using PostgreSQL
not: queues messages durably for sessions that are offline

cards.subject: Table partitioning
says: splits one large table into child tables by range, list or hash
lets queries skip partitions that cannot match
makes dropping old data a cheap partition drop
cards.use: manage a huge table where old rows are discarded by date
not: spreads the table across several servers automatically

cards.subject: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
says: runs the query and reports actual timings and row counts
shows where the plan's estimates differ from reality
executes writes for real when used on one
cards.use: find out why a query is slow
not: only prints the estimated plan without running anything

cards.subject: A Redis string
says: is the basic value type and can hold text, numbers or bytes
supports atomic increment on numeric values
can be set with an expiry in one command
cards.use: keep a counter or a cached blob
not: can only hold text shorter than one line

cards.subject: A Redis hash
says: maps field names to values under one key
suits an object with several attributes
lets you read or change one field without rewriting the rest
cards.use: store a user profile with separate fields
not: keeps its fields sorted by score

cards.subject: A Redis list
says: keeps ordered elements with push and pop at both ends
can act as a simple queue
is accessed by position, so the middle is slow to reach
cards.use: build a simple work queue
not: rejects duplicate elements

cards.subject: A Redis set
says: holds unique, unordered members
supports union, intersection and difference
answers membership in constant time
cards.use: track which users have already seen an item
not: keeps members in insertion order

cards.subject: A Redis sorted set
says: ties a numeric score to each unique member
returns members ordered by score or by rank
is the usual structure for a leaderboard
cards.use: build a leaderboard ranked by points
not: allows the same member twice with different scores

cards.subject: A Redis stream
says: is an append-only log of entries with generated ids
supports consumer groups that share the work
keeps entries until they are trimmed, unlike pub/sub
cards.use: need a durable event log with acknowledged consumption
not: drops a message once any subscriber has read it

cards.subject: Redis pub/sub
says: broadcasts messages to current subscribers of a channel
stores no messages
loses what a disconnected subscriber would have received
cards.use: push live notifications where missed messages are acceptable
not: replays missed messages to subscribers when they reconnect

cards.subject: Key expiry
says: deletes a key automatically after a time to live
is set with commands such as EXPIRE or SET with EX
is the basis of cache and session lifetimes
cards.use: want cached data to disappear on its own
not: must be run by a separate cleanup job you write

cards.subject: An RDB snapshot
says: saves a point-in-time copy of the dataset to a file
gives compact files that restart quickly
can lose writes made since the last snapshot
cards.use: want periodic compact backups of Redis
not: logs every single write command as it happens

cards.subject: An append-only file
says: logs every write command so it can be replayed
can be synced to disk every second or every write
is larger and slower to load than a snapshot
cards.use: want to lose at most about a second of Redis writes
not: is a point-in-time image taken at intervals

cards.subject: MULTI and EXEC
says: queue commands and run them as one uninterrupted sequence
do not roll back earlier commands if a later one fails at run time
are not the same as a relational transaction
cards.use: need several Redis commands to run without interleaving
not: undo all commands if any one fails

cards.subject: SET with NX
says: sets a key only if it does not already exist
is the building block of a simple lock
should be paired with an expiry so a crashed holder cannot block forever
cards.use: need only one worker to take a job
not: overwrites the existing value every time

cards.subject: An embedded database
says: runs inside the application process
needs no separate server to install or log into
stores its data in a local file
cards.use: want a database with nothing to operate
not: requires a network connection to a database server

cards.subject: SQLite's single-file storage
says: keeps a whole database in one file
can be backed up as one file when the copy is taken safely
ties the data to the machine that holds the file
cards.use: want a simple deployment with one file to back up
not: spreads tables over a cluster of nodes

cards.subject: SQLite's single writer
says: allows one write transaction at a time
lets many readers run alongside in WAL mode
becomes a bottleneck under heavy concurrent writes
cards.use: judge whether SQLite fits a write-heavy workload
not: allows many simultaneous writers on separate tables

cards.subject: SQLite WAL mode
says: appends changes to a separate log before merging them into the database file
lets readers continue while a writer writes
is turned on with a journal_mode pragma
cards.use: need readers not to block behind a writer
not: makes the database accept many concurrent writers

cards.subject: SQLite's foreign key pragma
says: turns on foreign-key enforcement
is off by default
must be set on each new connection
cards.use: find that orphan rows are being allowed
not: is stored permanently in the database file once set

cards.subject: SQLite's flexible typing
says: lets a column hold values of a different type than declared
relies on type affinity rather than strict types
can be tightened with strict tables
cards.use: want SQLite to reject text in an integer column
not: refuses any value that does not match the declared type

cards.subject: Drizzle ORM
says: describes tables in TypeScript code
infers query result types from that schema
supports PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite dialects
cards.use: want type-checked queries without writing a separate schema language
not: generates only raw SQL strings with no types

cards.subject: drizzle-kit generate
says: compares the schema to the last state and writes SQL migration files
produces files that can be reviewed and committed
does not change any database by itself
cards.use: need reviewable migrations that other environments will follow
not: syncs the schema straight to the database with no files

cards.subject: drizzle-kit push
says: applies the current schema directly to a database
leaves no migration history
suits fast local iteration
cards.use: are iterating quickly on a local database
not: writes numbered migration files for production

cards.subject: drizzle-kit migrate
says: applies generated migration files in order
records which migrations have run
is the step that makes shared databases follow the committed history
cards.use: need production to run the committed migration files
not: creates new migration files from schema changes

cards.subject: A MongoDB document
says: is a record made of field and value pairs, stored as BSON
can hold nested objects and arrays
always has a unique _id field
cards.use: store a record with nested data
not: must have the same fields as every other document in its collection

cards.subject: A MongoDB collection
says: is a group of documents
plays the role a table plays in a relational database
does not force its documents to share a shape by default
cards.use: decide where to put related documents
not: is a separate server instance

cards.subject: BSON
says: is the binary format MongoDB uses to store documents
adds types such as dates and binary data beyond plain JSON
encodes documents compactly for traversal
cards.use: wonder why MongoDB has a date type that JSON lacks
not: is a plain text format identical to JSON

cards.subject: An ObjectId
says: is a 12-byte identifier generated by default for _id
embeds a creation timestamp in its leading bytes
is created by the driver without asking the server
cards.use: need an id that sorts roughly by creation time
not: is guaranteed to be sequential with no gaps

cards.subject: Embedding documents
says: nests related data inside the parent document
reads parent and children in one fetch
gets awkward when the nested array grows without bound
cards.use: data is read together and the children are few
not: is the right way to model many-to-many relationships between large sets

cards.subject: Referencing documents
says: stores the id of a related document instead of its content
needs a second query or lookup to follow the link
avoids duplicating data that many parents share
cards.use: children are shared by many parents or grow without limit
not: is how a document store avoids ever needing a second read

cards.subject: The aggregation pipeline
says: passes documents through stages such as match, group and sort
does filtering and grouping on the server
is MongoDB's counterpart to SQL's grouping queries
cards.use: need totals per category from a collection
not: is a client-side loop over every document

cards.subject: A MongoDB replica set
says: keeps copies of the data on several nodes
elects a new primary if the current one fails
accepts writes only on the primary
cards.use: need MongoDB to survive the loss of a node
not: accepts writes on every member at once

cards.subject: MongoDB sharding
says: splits a collection across shards by a shard key
routes queries through a router process
is added for scale beyond one replica set
cards.use: see a collection outgrow a single replica set
not: is how MongoDB keeps copies for high availability

cards.subject: Schema validation in MongoDB
says: checks documents against rules when they are written
can use JSON Schema syntax
lets a flexible store still reject malformed data
cards.use: want a document store to refuse documents missing a required field
not: happens automatically with no rules being defined

cards.subject: An embedding
says: is a list of numbers that represents meaning
places similar content close together in vector space
is produced by a model
cards.use: need to compare texts by meaning rather than by words
not: is a compressed copy of the original text that can be decompressed

cards.subject: Vector similarity search
says: finds the stored vectors nearest to a query vector
returns results ranked by distance or similarity
finds matches by meaning rather than exact words
cards.use: want to find documents related to a question
not: matches only rows containing the exact query words

cards.subject: Cosine similarity
says: measures the angle between two vectors
ignores vector length
has a value near one for vectors pointing the same way
cards.use: compare embeddings regardless of their magnitude
not: measures the straight-line gap between two points

cards.subject: Euclidean distance
says: measures the straight-line gap between two vectors
is smaller for closer points
is sensitive to vector length
cards.use: need a distance where magnitude matters
not: measures only the angle between two vectors

cards.subject: Dot product
says: multiplies matching components and sums them
equals cosine similarity when vectors are normalised to length one
grows with vector length
cards.use: vectors are already normalised and speed matters
not: is always smaller than cosine similarity

cards.subject: Approximate nearest neighbour search
says: trades a little accuracy for much faster lookups
avoids comparing the query with every stored vector
may miss a true nearest neighbour
cards.use: search millions of vectors fast enough for a live request
not: guarantees the exact nearest vector every time

cards.subject: Exact nearest neighbour search
says: compares the query with every stored vector
always returns the true nearest vectors
slows down as the collection grows
cards.use: have a small collection and need perfect results
not: skips most vectors by using an index

cards.subject: An HNSW index
says: links vectors in layered proximity graphs
starts a search at a sparse top layer and moves down
trades memory and build time for fast, accurate queries
cards.use: need a graph index behind approximate search
not: buckets vectors by a hash of their first letter

cards.subject: Recall in vector search
says: is the share of true nearest neighbours the search actually returns
drops when the index is tuned for speed over accuracy
is measured against an exact search
cards.use: are checking how much an approximate index loses
not: is the time a query takes to return

cards.subject: A metadata filter
says: restricts vector search to items whose attributes match
applies conditions such as a tenant or a document type
is how one collection serves many users without mixing their results
cards.use: must return only one customer's data from a shared collection
not: changes the embedding of each stored item

cards.subject: A chunk
says: is a piece of a document embedded as one vector
is sized so it holds one idea
is retrieved on its own and passed to a model as context
cards.use: split a long document before embedding
not: is a whole document regardless of length

cards.subject: A vector collection
says: holds vectors of one fixed dimension
stores a payload alongside each vector
is where a distance metric is chosen
cards.use: set up a place to store embeddings
not: mixes vectors from different models freely

cards.subject: Re-embedding
says: is needed for all stored data when the embedding model changes
is required because vectors from different models are not comparable
is a reason to keep the source text next to the vectors
cards.use: decide to switch embedding models
not: can be skipped because old and new vectors line up

cards.subject: An inverted index
says: maps each term to the documents that contain it
makes finding documents by word fast
is the core structure of a search engine
cards.use: explain why full-text search is fast
not: maps each document to the list of its page numbers

cards.subject: An analyzer
says: breaks text into tokens and normalises them
runs at index time and at query time
decides how case and punctuation are treated
cards.use: want searches to ignore case and punctuation
not: ranks results by their relevance score

cards.subject: Stemming
says: reduces words to a root form
lets a search for run match running
can occasionally conflate unrelated words
cards.use: want plural and tense variants to match
not: corrects misspelled search terms

cards.subject: Fuzzy matching
says: tolerates a small number of character edits in a term
finds results despite typing mistakes
costs more than an exact term lookup
cards.use: want misspelled queries to still find results
not: reduces words to a shared root

cards.subject: BM25
says: scores a document by term frequency, term rarity and document length
gives rarer query terms more weight
is the default keyword relevance formula in many search engines
cards.use: explain how keyword search ranks results
not: compares the angle between embedding vectors

cards.subject: Hybrid search
says: combines keyword scores with vector similarity
catches exact terms that embeddings blur
merges two ranked lists into one
cards.use: need both exact-word and meaning-based matching
not: uses only the inverted index

cards.subject: Keyword search
says: matches the words in the query against indexed terms
finds exact names and codes reliably
does not understand synonyms by itself
cards.use: must find an exact part number
not: finds documents by the meaning of the query

cards.subject: Near-real-time refresh
says: makes new documents searchable after a short refresh interval
means a write is not visible instantly
is the reason a just-saved document may be missing from results
cards.use: see a new item missing from search for a moment
not: guarantees a document is searchable the moment it is written

cards.subject: A search index as derived data
says: is a copy built from the system of record
can be rebuilt from the source of truth
needs updating whenever the source changes
cards.use: decide where the authoritative copy of data should live
not: is the only place the data is stored

cards.subject: PostgreSQL full-text search
says: turns text into a tsvector and matches it with a tsquery
is usually backed by a GIN index
avoids running a separate search service for modest needs
cards.use: need decent text search without a new service
not: requires a separate engine to be installed

cards.subject: Cache-aside
says: has the application check the cache first and load from the database on a miss
fills the cache only for data that is requested
leaves the application responsible for updating or removing stale entries
cards.use: want the most common caching pattern with the app in control
not: has the cache itself fetch from the database on a miss

cards.subject: A read-through cache
says: loads missing data from the store through the cache layer
hides the database from the application code
keeps the loading logic inside the cache
cards.use: want the cache to handle misses itself
not: has the application load data on a miss

cards.subject: A write-through cache
says: writes to the cache and the database together
keeps the cache consistent with stored data
makes each write slower
cards.use: cannot tolerate a cache that lags behind writes
not: acknowledges writes before the database has them

cards.subject: A write-behind cache
says: acknowledges a write after updating the cache and saves to the database later
batches database writes
can lose acknowledged writes if the cache fails first
cards.use: want fast writes and accept a small loss window
not: updates the database before the cache

cards.subject: Cache invalidation
says: removes or refreshes entries when their source changes
is notoriously hard to get right
is easier when entries have a short lifetime
cards.use: change data that is also held in a cache
not: is handled by the database without any cache involvement

cards.subject: A cache stampede
says: occurs when many requests miss at once and all recompute the value
often follows the expiry of a popular key
is reduced by locking, early refresh or randomised lifetimes
cards.use: see a popular key expire and the database spike
not: is the removal of the least recently used entry

cards.subject: LRU eviction
says: removes the least recently used entry when the cache is full
assumes recently used data will be used again
needs a memory limit to be set
cards.use: decide what a full cache should drop
not: removes the oldest entry regardless of use

cards.subject: The cache hit ratio
says: is the share of lookups answered from the cache
shows whether the cache is worth its memory
drops when the working set exceeds the cache size
cards.use: measure whether a cache is helping
not: is the speed of the cache's network link

cards.subject: Negative caching
says: stores the fact that something does not exist
stops repeated lookups for missing items from reaching the database
needs a short lifetime so newly created items appear
cards.use: see repeated requests for ids that do not exist
not: caches only successful lookups

cards.subject: Primary-replica replication
says: sends writes to one primary and copies them to replicas
lets replicas serve reads
gives a standby that can be promoted
cards.use: want read scaling and a standby copy
not: lets every node accept writes

cards.subject: Synchronous replication
says: waits for a replica to confirm before acknowledging a write
avoids losing acknowledged writes on failover
adds latency and can stall when the replica is down
cards.use: cannot lose any acknowledged write
not: acknowledges the write before it leaves the primary

cards.subject: Asynchronous replication
says: acknowledges a write before replicas have it
keeps writes fast
can lose the last writes if the primary fails
cards.use: want the fastest writes and accept a small loss window
not: makes the primary wait for every replica

cards.subject: Replication lag
says: is the delay before a write reaches a replica
makes replica reads briefly stale
grows when replicas are overloaded
cards.use: see a user not find a record they just saved
not: is the time taken to start a new replica

cards.subject: Read-your-writes consistency
says: lets a client always see its own earlier writes
is often achieved by reading from the primary right after a write
can be broken by reading from a lagging replica
cards.use: want users to see their own edit immediately
not: guarantees every user sees every write at once

cards.subject: Failover
says: promotes a replica when the primary fails
should be tested before it is needed
with asynchronous replication may drop the latest writes
cards.use: lose the primary
not: restores a backup into an empty node

cards.subject: Split brain
says: occurs when two nodes both believe they are primary
can accept conflicting writes
is prevented by requiring a majority to elect a leader
cards.use: face a network partition that separates two halves of a cluster
not: is a node running out of disk space

cards.subject: Multi-primary replication
says: lets more than one node accept writes
needs a way to resolve conflicting updates
adds write availability at the cost of complexity
cards.use: must accept writes in several regions at once
not: has one write node and read-only copies

cards.subject: Hash sharding
says: places a row on a shard by hashing its shard key
spreads load evenly
makes range scans touch many shards
cards.use: want even distribution of writes
not: keeps adjacent keys together on one shard

cards.subject: Range sharding
says: assigns contiguous key ranges to shards
keeps range scans on few shards
can create a hot shard if keys grow monotonically
cards.use: want efficient scans over key ranges
not: spreads adjacent keys over all shards

cards.subject: A hot shard
says: is a shard receiving far more traffic than the others
often results from a poor shard key
limits scale to what one shard can handle
cards.use: see one node saturated while others idle
not: is a replica that is up to date

cards.subject: A shard key
says: decides which shard stores a row
should have many values and spread traffic
is hard to change after data exists
cards.use: design how rows will be distributed
not: is the key that encrypts data per shard

cards.subject: Consistent hashing
says: maps keys and nodes onto a ring
moves only a fraction of keys when a node is added or removed
avoids reshuffling nearly everything
cards.use: add a node to a cache cluster without massive remapping
not: assigns key ranges by alphabetical order

cards.subject: A quorum
says: is a majority of nodes needed to agree
guarantees reads overlap the latest write when reads plus writes exceed the node count
lets a cluster keep working with a minority down
cards.use: tune how many nodes must acknowledge
not: is any single node that responds first

cards.subject: Logical replication
says: copies row changes for chosen tables
can send a subset of data to another database
differs from byte-level copying of the whole cluster
cards.use: want to replicate only some tables
not: copies every byte of the storage files

cards.subject: Physical replication
says: ships the write-ahead log to copy the whole cluster
produces a replica identical at the storage level
cannot select individual tables
cards.use: want an exact standby of the whole server
not: replicates row changes for selected tables only

cards.subject: ACID
says: stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability
describes guarantees of a database transaction
is the model relational databases are known for
cards.use: need all-or-nothing updates with durable results
not: promises eventual consistency across replicas

cards.subject: BASE
says: stands for basically available, soft state and eventually consistent
favours availability over strict consistency
is contrasted with ACID
cards.use: describe a store that stays up and converges later
not: guarantees an immediate global ordering of all writes

cards.subject: The CAP theorem
says: says a partitioned system must choose between consistency and availability
applies when the network splits
is often misread as choose any two at all times
cards.use: reason about behaviour during a network partition
not: says a database may pick any two of three at all times and lose nothing

cards.subject: Eventual consistency
says: lets replicas disagree briefly
converges if updates stop
allows stale reads
cards.use: accept brief staleness for availability
not: guarantees every read sees the latest write

cards.subject: Strong consistency
says: makes every read return the latest committed write
costs latency, because replicas must coordinate
simplifies application reasoning
cards.use: cannot allow stale reads
not: allows replicas to disagree for a while

cards.subject: Linearizability
says: makes operations appear to take effect at a single instant
orders operations consistently with real time
behaves like a single copy of the data
cards.use: need the strictest single-object guarantee
not: only orders operations within one session

cards.subject: The read committed isolation level
says: lets a transaction see only committed data
can show different values for the same row within one transaction
is the default in PostgreSQL
cards.use: need protection from dirty reads at low cost
not: gives one fixed snapshot for the whole transaction

cards.subject: Snapshot isolation
says: gives each transaction a view as of its start
prevents non-repeatable reads
allows write skew
cards.use: need a stable view for a long read
not: is the same as serializable isolation

cards.subject: Write skew
says: happens when two transactions read the same data and update different rows, breaking a rule
can occur under snapshot isolation
is prevented by serializable isolation or explicit locks
cards.use: see two on-call doctors each go off duty at once
not: is a replica falling behind

cards.subject: Two-phase commit
says: has a coordinator ask all participants to prepare, then commit
can block participants if the coordinator fails
provides atomic commit across several stores
cards.use: need one atomic commit across two databases
not: lets each store commit independently with no coordination

cards.subject: The saga pattern
says: is a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions
gives up atomicity for availability
needs each step to be undoable
cards.use: coordinate a multi-service workflow without a distributed transaction
not: locks every service until all commit

cards.subject: An idempotent write
says: has the same effect when repeated
makes retries safe
is often done with a unique request key
cards.use: retry a request after a timeout
not: fails the second time it is run

cards.subject: Starting with PostgreSQL
says: is a safe default for most business applications
covers relational data, json, text search and queues at modest scale
delays the need for extra systems
cards.use: are choosing the first database for a new product
not: is wrong for any application with more than one table

cards.subject: Designing around the access pattern
says: starts from the queries and writes the system must serve
decides which store and keys fit
matters more than the data's apparent shape
cards.use: are unsure which store to pick
not: picks the store with the most features

cards.subject: A source of truth
says: is the one store whose copy wins when copies disagree
is written first and replicated to others
makes caches and search indexes rebuildable
cards.use: data lives in more than one place
not: is the fastest store in the system
like: A search index as derived data

cards.subject: Operational burden
says: covers backups, upgrades, monitoring and on-call for a store
grows with each additional technology
favours managed or embedded options for small teams
cards.use: watch a small team add yet another database
not: is ignored because installing a store is a one-time cost

cards.subject: The need for transactions
says: points towards a relational store when updates must succeed together
is costly to retrofit onto a store without them
should be decided early
cards.use: must update two records in a payment or neither
not: can be added later by changing a cache setting

cards.subject: Data volume and growth
says: asks how big data will be and how fast it grows
decides whether one node is enough
should be estimated rather than guessed from today's size
cards.use: plan capacity before choosing a store
not: is irrelevant once indexes exist

cards.subject: Lock-in
says: is the cost of leaving a vendor-specific store
grows with use of proprietary query features
is reduced by standard interfaces and exportable data
cards.use: weigh a cloud-only database against a portable one
not: disappears if the vendor is large enough

cards.subject: Managed versus self-hosted
says: trades control for less operational work
moves backups and patching to a provider
still leaves you responsible for restore tests and access control
cards.use: decide who patches and backs up the database
not: removes the need to ever test a restore

cards.subject: Ephemeral data
says: is data that can be lost and rebuilt
fits caches, sessions and counters
needs no durable backup
cards.use: decide what to put in an in-memory store
not: is data that legally must be kept for years

cards.subject: pg_dump
says: makes a logical backup of one PostgreSQL database
can write plain SQL or a custom archive format
is piped through gzip in a simple backup script
cards.use: take a quick logical backup of a PostgreSQL database
not: copies the data directory of the whole cluster

cards.subject: pg_restore
says: restores archives made by pg_dump in custom or directory format
can restore selected objects
is not used for plain SQL dumps
cards.use: restore a custom-format dump
not: replays a plain SQL file

cards.subject: pg_basebackup
says: takes a physical copy of the whole PostgreSQL cluster
is the starting point for a streaming replica
combines with archived WAL for point-in-time recovery
cards.use: set up a new replica or a physical backup
not: dumps one database as SQL

cards.subject: WAL archiving
says: saves completed write-ahead log segments elsewhere
lets a base backup be rolled forward to a chosen moment
is required for point-in-time recovery
cards.use: must restore to just before a bad delete
not: is a nightly dump of tables

cards.subject: mongodump
says: exports MongoDB data as BSON files
is restored with mongorestore
does not by itself give a consistent point in time on a busy cluster
cards.use: make a basic MongoDB backup
not: writes a plain SQL script

cards.subject: The SQLite backup command
says: copies a live database safely through the backup API
avoids a torn copy that a plain file copy risks during a write
writes the result as a normal database file
cards.use: back up a SQLite database that is in use
not: is a mysqldump option

cards.subject: VACUUM INTO
says: writes a compacted copy of a SQLite database to a new file
produces a consistent snapshot
is a simple way to take a backup
cards.use: want a clean single-file snapshot of SQLite
not: compacts the database in place without a copy

cards.subject: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
says: builds a PostgreSQL index without blocking writes
takes longer than a normal build
cannot run inside a transaction block
cards.use: add an index to a busy production table
not: locks the table against all writes until done

cards.subject: A migration history table
says: records which migrations have been applied
lets the tool run only the pending ones
keeps environments in step
cards.use: know which schema changes a database has
not: stores backups of the data

cards.subject: Expand and contract
says: adds the new structure first, moves data, then removes the old
keeps old and new application versions working during a deploy
avoids a breaking change in a single step
cards.use: rename a column without downtime
not: drops the old column and adds the new one in the same deploy

cards.subject: A restore drill
says: restores a backup into a scratch environment on a schedule
proves the backup is usable
measures how long recovery takes
cards.use: want to know a backup really works
not: checks only that the backup file exists

cards.subject: A zero-downtime migration
says: keeps the service available while the schema changes
splits a risky change into backward-compatible steps
avoids long locks on large tables
cards.use: change a large live table
not: takes the site offline for the duration

cards.subject: ggsocial's data store
says: is PostgreSQL accessed through Drizzle
describes tables in a TypeScript schema file
uses jsonb for flexible structured fields
cards.use: ask which database ggsocial uses
not: is a single SQLite file

cards.subject: gglearn's data store
says: is a single SQLite file read through better-sqlite3 and Drizzle
uses WAL mode and turns foreign keys on
runs as one process on one machine
cards.use: ask which database gglearn uses
not: is a PostgreSQL server in a container

cards.subject: ggmoney's database drivers
says: can run on SQLite or MySQL, chosen by DB_DRIVER
default to SQLite for development and tests
keep a separate migration folder for each engine
cards.use: ask how ggmoney supports two databases
not: are always PostgreSQL in production

cards.subject: ggmoney's MySQL strict mode
says: makes a truncated money value raise an error
guards against silent data damage that SQLite's flexibility would allow
is asserted by the deploy-check script
cards.use: worry about wrong values being stored quietly
not: is switched off so inserts never fail

cards.subject: Moksy's MongoDB layout
says: runs one MongoDB container for many services
gives each service its own named database
reads each connection string from MONGODB_URI
cards.use: ask how Moksy services keep data apart
not: shares one database among all services

cards.subject: Moksy's open-files limit
says: is raised in the compose file because Mongo ran out of file handles twice
follows from every service holding a connection pool
teaches sizing connections and limits as well as starting the container
cards.use: learn why Moksy raised a limit on its Mongo container
not: was added to speed up queries

cards.subject: Moksy's Qdrant service
says: is the vector database behind the AI memory feature
runs only in the ai and full profiles
has its own volume
cards.use: ask where Moksy keeps embeddings
not: is the store for permissions data

cards.subject: gglearn's in-memory rate limiting
says: keeps attempt counters in process memory
works while the app is one process
resets its counters on restart
cards.use: ask why gglearn needs no store for rate limiting
not: relies on a Redis cluster

cards.subject: ggsocial's database exposure
says: binds the Postgres container to 127.0.0.1 only
keeps data in a named volume so it survives container replacement
is never opened to the internet
cards.use: ask how ggsocial protects its database
not: publishes the Postgres port to all interfaces

qa.q: A team stores users and their orders and needs an order and its payment record to succeed or fail together. Which kind of store fits best?
qa.right: A relational database with transactions
wrong: A cache with a time to live
qa.why: Atomic multi-record updates are what transactions in a relational store provide.

qa.q: A product page is slow because the same row is read thousands of times a minute and changes once a day. What should the team add first?
qa.right: A cache in front of the database with an expiry
wrong: A second primary database accepting writes
qa.why: Mostly-read, rarely-changing data is the textbook case for a cache.

qa.q: Which Redis structure is the natural fit for a game leaderboard?
qa.right: A sorted set
qa.why: A sorted set keeps members ordered by score and returns rank cheaply.

qa.q: What does this command do?
qa.right: It sets the key only if it is absent, with a 30 second expiry
wrong: It overwrites the key and expires it after 30 minutes
It appends a value to a list for 30 seconds
It locks the whole database for 30 seconds
qa.why: NX means only if not present and EX gives seconds; together they form a simple expiring lock.

qa.q: A Redis instance restarts and some recent writes are gone, though snapshots exist. What explains it?
qa.right: Snapshots are taken at intervals, so later writes were not yet saved
wrong: Snapshots are encrypted and cannot be read
Redis deletes keys on every restart
qa.why: RDB snapshots are point-in-time, so writes after the last one can be lost.

qa.q: Which statement about Redis pub/sub is true?
qa.right: A subscriber that is offline misses messages published meanwhile
wrong: It retains a full history for new subscribers
qa.why: Pub/sub keeps no messages, which is why streams exist for durable consumption.

qa.q: A background worker must process each queued job once, and workers may crash mid-job. Which Redis feature suits this best?
qa.right: A stream with a consumer group and acknowledgements
wrong: A string holding the last job id
A set of finished jobs only
qa.why: Consumer groups track unacknowledged entries so crashed work can be claimed again.

qa.q: What does this query return on a table with a jsonb column named data?
qa.right: Rows whose data contains the key role with the value admin
wrong: Rows whose data has any key containing admin
Only the role column of each row
All rows, with data converted to text
qa.why: The @> operator tests containment and is supported by a GIN index.

qa.q: A query filters on a jsonb column with the containment operator and is slow on a large table. What helps most?
qa.right: A GIN index on the column
wrong: A B-tree index on the whole jsonb column for text search
qa.why: GIN indexes jsonb elements so containment avoids a full scan.
qa.code: CREATE INDEX idx_users_data ON users USING GIN (data);

qa.q: A heavily updated PostgreSQL table keeps growing although the row count is stable. Which is the most likely cause?
qa.right: Dead row versions are not being cleaned up fast enough
wrong: The planner statistics are too fresh
qa.why: MVCC leaves old versions that vacuum must reclaim.

qa.q: An app opens hundreds of connections per instance and PostgreSQL slows down. What is the standard fix?
qa.right: Put a connection pooler between the app and the database
qa.why: PostgreSQL spends a process per connection, so pooling keeps the count small.

qa.q: A team wants an exact standby copy of a whole PostgreSQL server. Which tool starts that?
qa.right: pg_basebackup
qa.why: A physical base backup is the starting point for a streaming replica.

qa.q: Which command is used to restore a custom-format archive made by pg_dump?
qa.right: pg_restore
wrong: psql with the archive piped in as SQL
qa.why: Custom and directory formats need pg_restore; plain SQL goes through psql.

qa.q: What does this command produce?
qa.right: A gzip-compressed plain SQL backup of one database
wrong: A physical copy of the cluster
qa.why: pg_dump writes SQL which is then compressed by gzip.

qa.q: Which statement about SQLite foreign keys is correct?
qa.right: Enforcement must be switched on for each connection
wrong: They are enforced only inside WAL mode
They cannot be used in SQLite
qa.why: The foreign_keys pragma is off by default and is per connection.

qa.q: A web app on SQLite has many readers and occasional writes, and readers sometimes wait behind a writer. Which setting reduces that?
qa.right: Turn on WAL journal mode
qa.why: In WAL mode readers continue while a writer writes.

qa.q: Which Drizzle command applies the committed migration files to a database?
qa.right: drizzle-kit migrate
qa.why: generate writes files; migrate runs them in order.

qa.q: A developer is changing the schema constantly on a local database and does not want migration files yet. Which command fits?
qa.right: drizzle-kit push
wrong: Editing the database file by hand
qa.why: Push syncs the schema directly with no history, suited to quick local work.

qa.q: Two environments must follow the exact same schema steps. Which Drizzle workflow should the team use?
qa.right: Generate migration files, commit them, and migrate each environment
wrong: Push from each developer's machine to production
Copy the SQLite file between servers
qa.why: Versioned migration files give every environment the same ordered history.

qa.q: A shared MongoDB product document has an ever-growing array of reviews. What is the safer model?
qa.right: Store reviews in their own collection and reference the product
wrong: Embed all reviews in the product document forever
Store reviews in a Redis list
qa.why: Unbounded arrays make documents large and slow; referencing avoids that.

qa.q: Which Mongo query returns documents whose status is active?
qa.right: db.orders.find({ status: "active" })
qa.why: find takes a filter document of field and value pairs.

qa.q: A Mongo service pipeline groups orders by customer and sums totals. What is this feature called?
qa.right: The aggregation pipeline
qa.why: Stages like $match and $group run on the server.

qa.q: Many services share one MongoDB and the server starts refusing connections with too many open files. What is the right response?
qa.right: Size connection pools and raise the file handle limit
wrong: Store everything in one service's database
qa.why: Each service's pool uses handles, so pools and limits must be sized together.

qa.q: Which description fits an embedding?
qa.right: A list of numbers where similar meanings are close together
wrong: A hash that is unique for each sentence
A compressed copy of the document
qa.why: Embeddings encode meaning so distance reflects similarity.

qa.q: Two embedding vectors are normalised to length one. Which statement is true?
qa.right: Their dot product equals their cosine similarity
wrong: Their Euclidean distance is always zero
Their dot product is always one
qa.why: With unit length the length term disappears from cosine.

qa.q: A vector index is tuned for speed and users report that a relevant document sometimes does not appear. What is being lost?
qa.right: Recall
qa.why: Approximate search can miss true nearest neighbours.

qa.q: A team changes its embedding model. What must they do with stored vectors?
qa.right: Re-embed all the source content with the new model
qa.why: Vectors from different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared.

qa.q: A multi-tenant assistant stores every customer's chunks in one collection. How is one customer's data kept from appearing for another?
qa.right: Apply a metadata filter on the tenant for every query
wrong: Rely on the embedding model to separate them
qa.why: Filtering on a tenant attribute restricts the search to that tenant's items.

qa.q: Users search a catalogue for exact part numbers and the semantic search keeps returning loosely related items. What is a good fix?
qa.right: Combine keyword search with vector search
qa.why: Hybrid search captures exact terms that embeddings blur.

qa.q: Why is a search engine's full-text lookup fast?
qa.right: It uses an inverted index from terms to documents
wrong: It scans every document on each query
It stores one row per character
It uses cosine similarity on every word
qa.why: Looking up the term gives the documents directly.

qa.q: A new product was saved but does not appear in search for about a second. What explains it?
qa.right: The index is refreshed near real time, not instantly
wrong: Search results are cached for a year
The inverted index only rebuilds nightly
qa.why: Near-real-time engines make writes searchable after a refresh interval.

qa.q: After changing an analyzer the old documents are not found by the new rules. What should the team do?
qa.right: Reindex the documents from the source of truth
qa.why: Analysis happens at index time, so existing entries must be rebuilt.

qa.q: A popular cached key expires and the database is suddenly overloaded by identical queries. What is this called?
qa.right: A cache stampede
qa.why: Many requests miss together and all recompute the value.

qa.q: Which change best reduces the chance of that problem?
qa.right: Add random jitter to expiry times and let one request refresh the value
wrong: Make every key expire at midnight
Raise the cache hit ratio target
qa.why: Staggered expiry and single refresh avoid simultaneous recomputation.

qa.q: In which pattern does the application look in the cache first, then load from the database on a miss?
qa.right: Cache-aside
qa.why: In cache-aside the application fills the cache itself.

qa.q: A cache acknowledges writes before saving them and then the cache node crashes. What was lost?
qa.right: Acknowledged writes not yet saved to the database
wrong: Nothing, writes are always persisted first
qa.why: Write-behind trades durability for speed.

qa.q: Users repeatedly request ids that do not exist and each request hits the database. Which technique helps?
qa.right: Negative caching with a short expiry
qa.why: Caching the absence stops repeated database lookups.

qa.q: A user saves a profile and the page reloaded from a replica shows the old values. What is the cause and a usual fix?
qa.right: Replication lag; read from the primary right after a write
qa.why: Replica reads can be stale; read-your-writes can be provided by reading the primary.

qa.q: A cluster is split by a network partition and both halves accept writes. What is this?
qa.right: Split brain
qa.why: Two primaries diverge; majority-based election prevents it.

qa.q: A team shards by creation date and one shard receives all new writes. What is this problem?
qa.right: A hot shard
qa.why: Monotonically growing keys concentrate load on the newest range.

qa.q: Which shard key is generally healthiest for evenly spreading writes?
qa.right: A high-cardinality key such as a user id hashed
qa.why: Many values and even traffic avoid hot shards.

qa.q: A cluster of three replicas requires two acknowledgements for writes and reads from two nodes. What does this guarantee?
qa.right: Reads overlap with the latest acknowledged write
wrong: Writes are never lost if all nodes fail
Reads are faster than a single node
Writes are stored on one node only
qa.why: Read and write quorums that sum above the node count must share a node.

qa.q: Which describes eventual consistency?
qa.right: Replicas may disagree for a time but converge if writes stop
wrong: Every read sees the newest write
Writes are applied in a single global order immediately
qa.why: Convergence is promised, not immediate agreement.

qa.q: What does the C in CAP mean?
qa.right: Every read sees the latest write or an error
qa.why: CAP's consistency is linearizable-style agreement across copies.

qa.q: During a network partition a system keeps answering from both sides with possibly stale data. Which choice did it make?
qa.right: Availability over consistency
qa.why: It chose to respond rather than refuse.

qa.q: Two doctors each check the on-call count, see two on duty, and each go off duty. Both transactions commit under snapshot isolation. What anomaly is this?
qa.right: Write skew
qa.why: Each wrote a different row, so the rule broke although neither conflicted directly.

qa.q: A payment spans two separate databases and must commit on both or neither. Which classic protocol does this?
qa.right: Two-phase commit
qa.why: A coordinator asks all to prepare and then commit.

qa.q: A booking spans three services that cannot share a transaction. A later step fails. How does a saga respond?
qa.right: Run compensating actions that undo the earlier steps
wrong: Lock all services until the failure clears
Roll back with a single database command
qa.why: Sagas rely on undoable local steps.

qa.q: A client retries a payment request after a timeout. Which design prevents a double charge?
qa.right: An idempotency key checked on the server
qa.why: A unique request key makes repeat requests have one effect.

qa.q: A new startup app with one team needs users, orders and simple search. Which choice is wisest?
qa.right: Start with PostgreSQL and add stores only when a need is shown
wrong: Use five specialised stores from day one
Use a graph database for everything
qa.why: One well-understood store keeps operation simple until real needs arrive.

qa.q: A team proposes adding Redis, a search engine and a graph database for a small app. What should you ask first?
qa.right: What access pattern does each one serve that the current database cannot?
wrong: Can they all be installed today?
qa.why: Each extra store adds operating cost and must justify itself.

qa.q: A search index and the main database disagree about a product's price. Which is correct?
qa.right: The source of truth, then rebuild the index from it
qa.why: Derived copies are rebuilt from the system of record.

qa.q: Which backup practice proves a backup works?
qa.right: Regularly restoring it into a scratch environment
wrong: Storing it on the same disk
qa.why: Only a restore shows the backup is usable.

qa.q: On a busy production table a team must add an index without blocking writes. Which statement should they run in PostgreSQL?
qa.right: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
wrong: CREATE INDEX with an exclusive lock at night
qa.why: The concurrent build allows writes during the build.
qa.code: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user ON orders (user_id);

qa.q: A column must be renamed while two app versions run during a deploy. Which approach is safest?
qa.right: Add the new column, copy data, move the app, then drop the old column
wrong: Rename the column in one migration
Drop the old column then add the new one
Take the database offline and restore a backup
qa.why: Expand and contract keeps both versions working throughout.

qa.q: ggmoney stores money as whole pence. Why does its MySQL schema use BIGINT?
qa.right: A plain INT would overflow at about 21.5 million pounds
wrong: BIGINT is faster for all queries
qa.why: Two billion pence is about 21.5 million pounds, so a larger integer is needed.

qa.q: Why does gglearn keep rate limit counters in process memory?
qa.right: The app runs as one process and the counters may reset on restart
wrong: Memory is more durable than files
qa.why: That design only works while there is a single process.

qa.q: Which statement about the ggsocial production database is correct?
qa.right: Postgres runs in a container bound to 127.0.0.1 with a named volume
wrong: The Postgres port is open to the internet
Data is stored in the container layer only
It runs from a SQLite file
qa.why: Binding locally avoids exposure and the volume keeps data across container replacement.
